📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

It has been revealed that at the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

In a recent development, this already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Industry observers note that of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

Recent findings suggest that there are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Industry observers note that critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Sources indicate that until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease.
  • According to recent reports, the research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's.
  • According to recent reports, "These findings break upcoming ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A gene that helps the brain contain harmful protein buildup may play a crucial role in Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that when this gene stops functioning properly, the brain's natural defenses become less effective, allowing toxic plaques to accumulate more rapidly. The findings could point toward new ways to detect, treat, or potentially prevent the disease.

According to recent reports, the research, led by John Lukens, PhD, focused on a gene called CASS4, which previous studies had repeatedly linked to an increased risk of Alzheimer's. Until now, however, scientists knew little about what the gene actually does. The team discovered that CASS4 helps regulate microglia, specialized immune cells that act as the brain's cleanup and defense system. When the gene's activity was disrupted, these cells struggled to respond to harmful plaques. They also became much less effective at containing and compacting the toxic material, allowing the plaques to expand and spread more aggressively.

According to recent reports, "These findings break upcoming ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer's disease," said Lukens, director of UVA's Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases. "Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer's and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease.".

How the Brain's Cleanup System Protects Against Alzheimer's.

More than 6 million Americans are living with Alzheimer's, a progressive disease that gradually damages memory and thinking abilities. As the condition advances, people can lose the ability to recognize even their closest family members, including their own children. Alzheimer's is the sixth-leading cause of death in the United States, according to the figures cited by the researchers.

It has been revealed that two major changes in the brain are associated with the disease. One is the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques, sticky deposits of protein that collect between nerve cells. The other is the formation of twisted tangles of a protein called tau. Both are hallmarks of Alzheimer's, but growing evidence suggests that the brain's immune system, particularly its microglia, also plays an vital role in how the disease develops.

Sources indicate that microglia normally help protect the brain by responding to threats and managing harmful material. When amyloid-beta plaques appear, these immune cells can surround them with protective barriers and compress the deposits into smaller, more tightly packed structures. This containment process helps limit the damage the plaques can cause to surrounding brain tissue.

The UVA researchers found that CASS4 is crucial for maintaining this protective response. When the gene was disrupted in laboratory mice, microglia became less capable of controlling amyloid-beta plaques. As a result, the plaques accumulated more rapidly, nearby nerve cells called neurons suffered damage, and the animals experienced worsening cognitive function.

A Little-Known Alzheimer's Gene Reveals Its Role.

Recent findings suggest that "Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer's risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper," said Addie Walsh, UVA physiology graduate student and first author of the paper. "These are notable findings because they give us upcoming insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology.".

The researchers also discovered that losing CASS4 set off a series of changes in the activity of other genes. These widespread effects could have implications beyond Alzheimer's, potentially helping explain biological processes involved in other neurodegenerative diseases, which progressively damage nerve cells.

Industry observers note that one of the most significant findings was where CASS4 appears to exert its influence. Scientists had previously suspected that the gene contributed to Alzheimer's primarily through its effects on neurons, the cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain. Instead, the latest research indicates that its main role is in the immune system.

Recent findings suggest that that distinction could be key for developing future treatments. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate in Alzheimer's, researchers may be able to strengthen the immune cells that help protect the brain from those deposits. The UVA team believes that increasing CASS4 activity or improving microglial function could eventually offer ways to slow or prevent the disease.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer's Treatments.

Industry observers note that "We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it," stated Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. "Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer's. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential.".

According to recent reports, the findings suggest that the brain's immune defenses may offer an crucial opportunity for future Alzheimer's therapies. They also raise the possibility that defective CASS4 activity could eventually serve as an early warning sign of the disease, potentially helping doctors identify people at risk before more serious symptoms develop.

Recent findings suggest that however, these possibilities remain to be tested. The experiments showing increased plaque buildup, neuronal damage, and cognitive decline were conducted in mice. Further research will be needed to determine whether targeting CASS4 can produce similar protective effects in humans.

In a recent development, the work is part of a broader effort at UVA to translate laboratory discoveries into treatments for serious diseases. Lukens leads the Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer's and Neurodegenerative Diseases, which operates within UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute was created to accelerate the development of medicines and other therapies for complex medical conditions using advances from UVA's biomedical research programs.

Lukens is also a member of UVA's Center for Brain Immunology and Glia (SIGNIFICANT Center), which studies the roles of immune cells and other supporting cells in brain health and disease.

Walsh, meanwhile, is preparing to continue her research into the brain's immune system in a new position.

"I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical manufacturer Novartis," she said. "I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration.".

Alzheimer's Gene Discovery Published in Scientific Journal.

According to recent reports, the research was published in the Journal of Experimental Medicine. The authors are Adeline E. Walsh, Benjamin A. Davis, Joshua D. Samuels, William A. Mills III, Jessica M. Thanos, Alexis M. Johnson, Katelyn A. Moore, Michael A. Puchalski, Eric J. Steacy, Benjamin W. Wendell, Amélie Daugherty-Lopès, Adrian A. Shimpi, Ukpong B. Eyo and Lukens. The researchers reported having no financial interest in the work.

Among the contributors is Davis, a fourth-year biology student at UVA, who says participating in scientific research has helped shape his approach to problem-solving and his plans for a career in medicine.

"I think that undergraduate research develops a kind of critical thinking that is difficult to cultivate inside a classroom," he remarked. "My experience with research has taught me to approach questions systematically and never assume there will be a clear answer. As I prepare to apply to medical school, I know these experiences will shape how I approach clinical care and the broader field of science.".

Recent findings suggest that funding came from the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging through grants R01AG071996, R01AG087406, RF1AG078684 and R01AG086344. Additional support was provided by the Cure Alzheimer's Fund, the Owens Family Foundation, the Harrison Family Foundation, the Rick Sharp Foundation, and the Steven A. Newman AD Award.

10 Best Metroidvania Boss Fights of the 2020s (So Far)

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Modern Metroidvanias, largely influenced by Soulsborne titles' formula, have heavily emphasized boss fights as the core of their gameplay, and I'm quite happy about it.
  • I can't deny my absolute fascination with formidable adversaries that test my reflexes, adaptability, and resolve, and this genre in particular has understood those keys better than most.
  • With each passing year, we not only receive more outstanding Metroidvanias but also specifically more experiences that utilize this gameplay concept to its fullest potential, usually representing the high points of their respective adventures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Modern Metroidvanias, largely influenced by Soulsborne titles' formula, have heavily emphasized boss fights as the core of their gameplay, and I'm quite happy about it.

I can't deny my absolute fascination with formidable adversaries that test my reflexes, adaptability, and resolve, and this genre in particular has understood those keys better than most.

With each passing year, we not only receive more outstanding Metroidvanias but also specifically more experiences that utilize this gameplay concept to its fullest potential, usually representing the high points of their respective adventures.

Therefore, if you're like me and fascinated by a good duel with health bars and numerous phases, I invite you to read this list of the ten best Metroidvania boss fights of the 2020s (so far).

Well Dweller is a magnificent video game that, as the pinnacle of Kyle Thompson's craft, is brimming with spectacular yet accessible special bosses, such as The Queen.

The plethora of sequences, attacks, and projectiles that unfold during your final encounter is breathtaking, truly connecting with the idea that royalty rules with an iron fist because they actually possess the power to dominate others.

Disfiguring the face of your family's kidnapper is fitting for a title that's cozy on the surface but profoundly dark beneath it, materialized in a demanding fight in terms of positioning and movement that makes you feel like you're constantly swimming against the tide.

While the bosses in Well Dweller wouldn't be my primary reason for recommending this gem, The Queen, in particular, demonstrates the wide variety that Metroidvanias can offer, rather than simply reducing everything to dodging and attacking in between.

The entirety of Shinobi: Art of Vengeance is a moving marvel with choreography worthy of the best action sequences of recent years, thanks to the tremendous animations and magnificent display of audiovisual effects for bosses like Lord Ruse.

Its imposing arena and visual design provide the perfect backdrop to prepare you for the epic duel this tormented villain has in store, whose tragic origin story is only surpassed by the way his darkness permeates the fight.

What was once an honorable man surrenders his body and mind to an abject power that threatens the balance of the world, making it fitting that his fight resembles that of a ninja against a natural phenomenon capable of defying the laws of physics.

The gameplay is very satisfying, forcing you to use all the tools and combos at your disposal to evade and attack effectively, leveraging the title's glorious combat system, where, after dominating all the combos, you can truly perform a martial aesthetic feast.

The gimmick of having you constantly face a boss throughout a game is quite difficult to pull off successfully, but Gilroy, the Administrator from Ender Magnolia: Bloom in the Mist is a perfect example of when it's done well.

While the game's roster of bosses is quite varied, its developers understand the magic of fighting a humanoid adversary who, true to FromSoftware's philosophy, forces you to decipher a rapid and relentless attack pattern where the slightest mistake is punished with death.

Gilroy is a challenge that evolves in each of the three encounters, always leaving room for more secrets, until the final confrontation arrives with the full weight of the narrative, where you must fight one last battle that is as bittersweet as it is satisfying.

Ender Magnolia is a game that relies heavily on its aesthetics, story, and music to amplify its emotional impact, so the campaign reaches its peak when you must defeat this recurring and memorable figure one last time.

Speaking of recurring tropes throughout video game history, Tunic presents The Heir as the final boss very early in the story, allowing you to become familiar with its power while simultaneously understanding how far you are from completing your journey.

Games with such a strong emphasis on exploration and adventure as this one must make every element contribute to the sense of progress, and nothing demonstrates your growth more than a superpowered entity with whom you gradually close the gap.

Checking your evolution through repeated attempts over many hours is captivating, as is finally realizing you're on par and understanding the remarkable challenge it truly holds, hidden behind complex and rapid combos, diverse area attacks, and far more resistance than you initially expected.

The Heir's fight is simple but makes the most of Tunic's functional mechanics, and the satisfaction of delivering the final blow after so many hours lost and disoriented is unparalleled.

Ori and the Will of the Wisps constantly surpasses itself with each upcoming boss, escape sequence, and scene, culminating in a Shriek encounter that ranges from breathtaking to utterly devastating.

The franchise is a relentless litany of tragedies and victims that exact a toll on the kindness of those who suffer them, leading you to confront a majestic yet deeply traumatized owl amidst what appears to be the end of the universe.

The screen seems to crumble as your confrontation with Shriek unfolds dynamically, with both combat and platforming sections taking place as the boss moves in and out of the frame with truly enviable dynamism.

More than just a boss fight, the sequence feels like a genuine battle where a force of nature truly wants to defeat you; sensations enhanced by the magnificent soundtrack and the sheer madness of particles and colors displayed during the fight.

Fighting Vahram in his godlike form inside the borders of time itself is among those images that stay with you forever, something Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown does quite regularly.

These former brothers-in-arms clash in a magnificent duel where time freezes and reverses, beams of light and swords appear from all sides, and your adversary manipulates the laws of physics as if they were clay, making it a truly spectacular show.

As you whittle down his health and he becomes cornered, the fight's complexity increases considerably, building to a tremendous crescendo where you feel the climax approaching and the adrenaline surging.

Vahram is one of those bosses who can destroy you dozens of times in a row and you'll still be happy, because he's so well and precisely designed that each upcoming opportunity to fight him again feels like a gift.

True final bosses are usually the ultimate display of difficulty, depth, and passion that a Metroidvania has to offer, including Shii in MIO: Memories in Orbit.

Fighting the companion who guided you throughout the story not because of some villainous adversity, but because of a genuine conflict of beliefs about what constitutes the most desirable outcome, is heartbreaking yet captivating, especially given the challenge that awaits.

Shii lives up to his title, offering a multi-layered duel that demands you be as adept at recognizing openings as you are at dodging, jumping, dashing, grappling, flying, and more to evade its endless array of varied and omnidirectional attacks.

The boss also flies, vanishes, glides, and crawls in an organic clash that makes the most of MIO: Memories in Orbit's environment and mechanics, resulting in an absolute delight.

Blasphemous 2 boasts one of the most fluid and satisfying combat systems in the entire genre, but none exploit its flow state's sweet satisfaction quite like Eviterno, Last Desecrator.

While the rest of the game is relatively manageable, this timeless warrior subverts expectations and delivers the beating of your life, proving that all the challenges you've overcome so far were just the tip of the iceberg he embodies.

Far from the abominations and colossi you face during your crusade, the title presents, in its climax, a knight equal to you whose speed, power, and versatility demand pixel-perfect decision-making every second, regardless of your build.

The best bosses are the ones that push you to your limits, and considering Eviterno penalizes even a millisecond off-timing or being a pixel too close, he's a clear contender for the decade's finest.

Eigong is a mentor to our protagonist in Nine Sols both in story and gameplay, as no other encounter teaches you to appreciate its prodigious combat system so profoundly.

There are fierce contenders throughout the campaign, though the one tasked with opposing Yi at the very end exponentially raises the demands of mechanical control, as any performance less than perfect will result in the same outcome: a return to the checkpoint.

With three hellish phases brimming with rapid and agile movements—horizontal and vertical, parryable and unparryable, close and long range—it's an unstoppable barrage of abilities unless you know Yi's powers like the back of your hand.

Only absolute, unwavering concentration will give you a chance against Eigong, whose defeat swiftly transforms from a painful climb into one of the most magical memories a Metroidvania has ever offered.

Being the only one on the entire list who isn't the game's final boss, which already hints at her unparalleled quality, Skarrsinger Karmelita is Hollow Knight: Silksong's highest point.

That Team Cherry's masterpiece has the genre's best boss this decade is undeniable, with representatives like Trobbio, Second Sentinel, Cogwork Dancers, and Lace to justify it, but ultimately it's the queen of the ants who gets the recognition.

It's a majestic encounter from the very beginning, leading you through the halls of a theater with her glorious singing, and then, after gifting you her minions as an offering to start the fight with full silk, appearing on stage to give you the concert of your life.

The song, setting, art direction, attacks, rhythm, duration... Everything is perfectly timed to ensure a flawless experience, whether it takes you one try or a thousand (which is more likely).

Skarrsinger Karmelita, I dare say, is among the best bosses in video game history and a perfect example of why this gameplay concept has gained so much relevance over the years.

Industry News: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult.
  • Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis.
  • The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, yet recognizing the disease early can be difficult. Its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions, including kidney stones, allowing warning signs to go unnoticed.

Researchers at the University of Plymouth have now developed an artificial intelligence system that could help doctors identify people at risk of bladder cancer years before they receive a diagnosis. In some patients, the technology detected subtle warning signals dating back as far as five years.

The new approach uses AI to examine electronic health records, searching for combinations of symptoms, medical conditions, risk factors, and healthcare activity that might otherwise be overlooked. By recognizing these patterns, researchers hope to make bladder cancer screening more accurate and help doctors find the disease when treatment is most likely to succeed.

AI Finds Hidden Bladder Cancer Clues in Medical Records.

In a recent development, under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs of bladder cancer is visible blood in the urine (hematuria). However, blood in the urine can also result from noncancerous problems, including kidney stones and prostate conditions. This overlap makes it difficult to determine which patients need further investigation and contributes to missed cases.

It has been revealed that confirming bladder cancer presently requires a procedure called cystoscopy (where a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder). Although effective, the examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients who are most likely to have the disease.

To explore a possible solution, a team led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients. The records covered a 25-year period, from 1995 through 2020.

In a recent development, the researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators (from smoking and exercise habits to medication use). From this enormous collection of information, the system narrowed the list to 38 features that were especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk.

AI Identifies 85% of Bladder Cancer Cases.

The results suggest that AI could substantially improve the way patients are assessed for bladder cancer.

It has been revealed that the model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not have the disease. It also performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

Importantly, the system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis. Some of the warning signals it recognized could be traced back up to five years, suggesting that valuable clues may exist in medical records long before cancer is discovered.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors, including smoking and blood in the urine. However, it also uncovered unexpected associations that conventional screening approaches would be unlikely to detect.

Industry observers note that for example, patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appeared to have a lower risk of bladder cancer. Meanwhile, long-term use of tamoxifen (a breast cancer medication) was associated with a higher risk.

It has been revealed that these findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it. Instead, they raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms that researchers believe deserve closer examination.

Another surprising finding involved blood in the urine. Although this symptom is often considered a major warning sign, its significance appears to depend partly on a patient's other medical conditions. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, for instance, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk.

Understanding these relationships more fully could eventually help doctors distinguish patients who need urgent investigation from those who may not require invasive testing.

A New Approach to Early Cancer Screening.

Beyond identifying warning signs, the AI system could also divide patients into three groups according to their estimated likelihood of having bladder cancer: low-risk (below 7% probability), uncertain (grey zone: 7-55%), and high-risk (above 55%).

This approach could help healthcare providers decide which patients need immediate attention and which may benefit from additional monitoring.

In a recent development, for example, patients in the uncertain category might be monitored before undergoing procedures such as cystoscopy. If further research confirms the system's reliability, this could reduce unnecessary examinations while allowing doctors to concentrate resources on people at greatest risk.

PhD student Xu Wang, who led the data analysis, said: "Bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022.".

In a recent development, "Despite its prevalence, no routine screening program exists for the general population, and - following symptoms - detection relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Our system goes far beyond traditional symptoms, and it's great to have uncovered the results that we have. The research shows that the combination of multiple factors - from medication histories to seemingly unrelated conditions - can reveal patterns invisible to conventional screening methods.".

Could AI Help Doctors Catch Bladder Cancer Earlier?

Sources indicate that the potential benefits extend beyond improving diagnostic accuracy. Detecting bladder cancer earlier could mean more treatment options, better survival outcomes, and fewer patients undergoing invasive procedures unnecessarily.

Industry observers note that dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, emphasized the importance of developing better screening methods.

"Bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families.

"It could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier, when survival outcomes and quality of life can be dramatically improved.".

Professor Shang-Ming Zhou believes the findings point toward a more individualized approach to cancer screening, in which AI helps doctors interpret a patient's broader medical history rather than relying primarily on individual symptoms.

"This work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

"By harnessing the power of interpretable machine learning and comprehensive health records, we're moving closer to detecting this disease at its earliest, most treatable stages.".

More Research Needed Before Clinical Use.

Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use.

Sources indicate that all the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Before the model can be introduced into other healthcare settings, researchers will need to determine whether it performs equally well with different patient populations and medical record systems.

Professor Zhou explained why broader testing is essential.

"It's important to emphasize that further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely - for example, all of the data analyzed came from the SAIL database in Wales, so we'd want to investigate other datasets too.

Sources indicate that "But it's a very exciting early study. Additional studies would also be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions.".

The findings offer an encouraging glimpse of how artificial intelligence might improve cancer screening by uncovering patterns hidden within years of routine medical information. With further validation, such tools could help doctors recognize bladder cancer sooner, prioritize patients who need testing, and potentially improve outcomes.

The study, "Early Detection of Bladder Cancer Using Advanced Feature Engineering and Swarm Intelligence Optimization on EHRs," was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering.

The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

Xbox leader Asha Sharma has alluded to harnessing the power of generative AI when making games, in a memo published this afternoon.

The memo, titled 25 years of Xbox, charts the growth of Microsoft from small beginnings through to the thousands-strong company it is today. But it's Sharma's comments at the end of the memo that are of particular interest.

While talking about what the next 25 years could bring, Sharma lamented that "too many ideas never become games" and that "too many games fall short of what their creators imagined". "For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition," she wrote. "We must change this.".

Recent findings suggest that sharma continued: "Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today's games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982.".

According to recent reports, there is no explicit mention of generative AI here, but the language is suggestive - "a single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations". Furthermore, Asha's memo follows last month's announcement of an Xbox Labs initiative that also sounded like it was based around generative AI, despite avoiding the phrase specifically.

This isn't a surprise, of course. Microsoft as a wider company is all-in on generative AI, with Copilot, and Sharma's background at Microsoft is in AI. But it's an area she's avoided speaking too enthusiastically about since her hiring as Xbox boss earlier this year. At the time, Sharma stated she has "no tolerance for bad AI", and there's been such a lot else going on in the months since - including wide-ranging restructuring resulting in the loss of thousands of Xbox jobs - that the topic of generative AI has fallen into the background. Perhaps now we're seeing the sprouting seeds of it.

It has been revealed that shopify Rebellion Black opened the North America Qualifier Playoffs with a 2-0 win over Xora Esports. The non-partner organisation is now one win from the playoffs that decide a guaranteed São Paulo Kickoff place.

The best-of-three Group Stage meeting with Xora began at 00:10 UTC on Saturday 21 November, opening Shopify Rebellion Black’s VCT Americas Kickoff: North America 2027 campaign.

The result counts for more because Shopify Rebellion is now outside Riot’s partnership system. The organisation was one of the Americas sides that mentioned it had not been chosen for the 2027-2028 partnership programme, Sheep Esports reported. Cloud9, ENVY, M80, FlyQuest and LYON were also on that list. Riot now has eight partner teams in each of its four regions.

The Swiss Stage runs from 20 to 22 November 2026. Every match is best of three. Two wins send a team through to the playoffs, and two losses knock it out. The eight teams left after the Swiss phase move into a double-elimination bracket played over six competition days, with the playoffs set for 1 to 6 December. The event is listed as an online, A-Tier Riot Games qualifier for 16 teams.

According to recent reports, shopify Rebellion Black’s next opponents are Oafs, who also won their opening match 2-0, against QoR. Both teams are therefore one win from the playoffs. Oafs already have a record against Xora. They knocked them out of the Qualifier 1 bracket on 8 November with a 2-1 win. Xora had still reached the Qualifier Playoffs by finishing joint third in the 512-team North America Qualifier 1.

Across 83 rated matches, Shopify Rebellion Black hold a 59-24 record. Before this event their most recent series was a 2-3 defeat to 2GAME Esports at the VCL Americas Last Chance Qualifier 2026. Earlier in that event they had beaten 2GAME Esports 2-1 and Contra 2-0.

Recent findings suggest that the organisation’s second line-up had a harder start. Shopify Rebellion Gold lost 0-2 to Maryville University. Several of the other organisations left out of the partnership programme won their first matches. Cloud9 beat counterfeit 2-0, Team Envy beat Yellow Dragon Gaming 2-0 and FlyQuest edged Masterclass 2-1. Elsewhere, Winthrop University beat SaD Esports 2-0 and YFP Gaming beat Wildcard 2-1.

According to recent reports, the prize for coming through the bracket is a place in São Paulo. Riot will stage the 2027 VCT Americas Kickoff in Brazil. Its eight Partner Teams get direct entry. Non-partner teams can win four places: one guaranteed slot each for North America, Brazil and Latin America, plus one for the Americas Last Chance Qualifier. For a non-partner side, a later run to Masters would be worth a fixed US$200,000 and a place at Champions US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. The regional Kickoff events are due to start on 14 January 2027 and run until 7 February 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that warning: I'm probably about to make you feel old. Today, November 11th 2026, is the 15th anniversary of Skyrim's release. The first one, before it was re-released on every other platform under the sun. Fittingly, one of its best expansion mods, Beyond Skyrim: Bruma, has gotten a beefy 2.0 update to commemorate the occasion. Though, its creators insist the main driving force behind the update was more a matter of "technical necessity". There are new quests, dungeons, and corners of Skyrim-era Cyrodiil to explore either way.

"You might ask yourself why, after all these years, we have put any more work into polishing and even adding newly introduced content to Bruma," the Beyond Skyrim team wrote in an article about the making of their version of Bruma's 2.0 update. "We are, of course, working on the whole province of Cyrodiil, and have made significant progress which you can follow on our social media. With so much still to go however, it was not out of nostalgia for a 15 year old Skyrim or a nearly 10 year old Bruma that we decided to revisit the first, and as of the time of writing, only major Beyond Skyrim release.

In a recent development, "The reason for this update is actually a technical necessity," the modders continued. "The problem we have with Bruma is that it is based on a very very old version of Cyrodiil, which had been branched off of the main development build of Cyrodiil soon after Bruma's initial release in 2017. Whenever we updated Bruma, that meant we had to merge our changes into two builds, the public Bruma build and the WIP Cyrodiil build." So, in order to solve that behind-the-scenes problem, the team have developed a "build stripper" tool which means they'll not have to juggle maintaining two builds going forwards.

In a recent development, as laid out in the showcase video above, the modders have also used Bruma 2.0 as an opportunity to overhaul and add to vast chunks of their recreation of Cyrodiil's northernmost county. A fully voiced quest called All The Wrong Places which was cut from the mod's initial release, "several fresh dungeons and interiors", and an expansion of the explorable area all grace the changelog.

Sources indicate that more clothing, armour, weapons including the mod's first spear, enemies, spells, enchantments, world encounters, books, and treasure maps have also been shipped in with the 2.0 version, alongside overhauls to boss fights. A fresh opening title splash will greet you upon entering Bruma for the first time, you should benefit from higher FPS as you explore the city, and the modders have even added an apple to Jerall View Inn. That's far from the end of the tweaks, so it's well worth reading the full list if you've got time.

In a recent development, "All in all, Bruma 2.0 has been a massive journey, one where we have built and learned a lot, and most importantly, made many advancements to prepare us for the future," the modders concluded. If you've not given Beyond Skyrim: Bruma a go, I can very much recommend it. You might find yourself wandering back across the border into Skyrim once you've had your fill of nostalgia-tinged exploration and staring at a distant Imperial City you can't visit, but the original version's still good for hours of extra Elder Scrollsing.

You can grab the 2.0 version of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma from Nexus Mods. It's worth noting that you'll need "a recent version (1.6 or higher) of Skyrim: Special Edition's upgrade.esm and update.bsa" and a separate mod containing Beyond Skyrim's shared asset repository. Saves made using previous versions of Beyond Skyrim: Bruma won't work with the 2.0 update, so it's likely worth starting a new playthrough or relying on an in-progress one you've yet to use any mods with.

#132190. AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1331 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed.
  • For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works.
  • But the latest findings raise an crucial question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A upcoming study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.

But the latest findings raise an crucial question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?

"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a upcoming study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity.".

A Fresh Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI.

The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.

Sources indicate that if these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.

In a recent development, "Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," states Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.

The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.

Industry observers note that their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.

AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story.

The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.

In a recent development, AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.

"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.

The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.

Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.

That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.

According to recent reports, "The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," states Kar.

Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior.

The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.

If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.

According to recent reports, "Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," claims Muzellec.

Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.

In a recent development, the concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.

Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain.

Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.

By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.

"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially crucial for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline.".

A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.

To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.

Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.

The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.

📅 06 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vg247

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HoYoverse just wrapped up a massive Honkai: Star Rail Special Program.
  • In a recent development, the upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason.
  • It has been revealed that planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HoYoverse just wrapped up a massive Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

In a recent development, the upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the massive new world headlining Version 4.0.

It has been revealed that planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

Sources indicate that the imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

Industry observers note that the Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

It has been revealed that much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

According to recent reports, as you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Recent findings suggest that version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other latest arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

It has been revealed that she also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that heartopia has officially shared initial details about its first-ever collaboration event. The game, which released a month ago to great success on mobile, as well as Steam on PC, has already been a staple among fans of Animal Crossing and The Sims.

Things are kicking into gear, it seems, because the game is already about to host its first collaboration event, and it is with My Little Pony.

The Heartopia X My Little Pony event officially begins on February 14, but a pre-launch login event is now live through the actual collaboration’s start. The limited-time event offers players sign-in puzzles every day that will unlock time-limited Exhibition Passes.

According to recent reports, the first actual piece of My Little Pony-themed content can be yours if you complete all puzzles, as that gets you a limited edition costume for your pet, based on the show’s Spike. The event itself, which will be available until March 15, brings My Little Pony’s Tree of Harmony into the world of Heartopia.

Sources indicate that the ponies need your help to Wield Elements of Harmony so they can reawaken the tree, and bring it back to Equestria. In gameplay terms, you’re going to want to perform daily sensing at the tree in order to earn three of the six Elements of Harmony: Honesty, Generosity, Loyalty, Kindness, Laughter, and Magic.

The more you do this, the more the tree’s Energy goes up, and the more rewards and resources you stand to earn. Even more time-limited Exhibition Passes, and Moonlight Crystals can be earned as you water the tree.

According to recent reports, badge Pull Tokens are your big reward, which is what you’re actually going to use to get the special Pony Series badges. You’ll earn ten time-limited Exhibition Passes each time you complete one of the three sets of Pony Series badges. Collect all three and you’ll earn Town Collaboration Series badges.

In a recent development, heartopia is a free-to-play game, so you know there is a Gacha component to this event. Expect six non-replacement Gacha Pools that each map to one member of My Little Pony’s Mane Six. Within each pool, you’ll be able to earn five outfit pieces, and one vehicle.

We also recently updated our guides on how to catch Frostspore fish - and if you’re into cooking, how to obtain every recipe and variant. If you haven’t already, definitely see if you missed any of these Heartopia codes, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last night, Xbox Game Studios and Halo Studios have announced a free revision for the recently-released Halo: Campaign Evolved, which promises to add the four-player co-operative PvE mode, Firefight, to the game.

"For nearly two decades, Firefight has been a Halo favorite, challenging Spartans to team up, hold the line, and survive wave after wave of enemies," claims Halo Studios director of competitive engagement Tahir Hasangjekaj said in a dedicated post on the Xbox website. "The tradition continues this winter as we add the four-player cooperative PvE mode to Halo: Campaign Evolved in a free update.".

Though we don't have a release date for the update yet, Hasangjekaj does explicitly state "this Winter" as a window, and promises that we'll hear more information about the update at Halo Fest - due to run from 12th to 13hth December in Seattle, Washington. My money would be on a release around then, therefore.

"We're kicking things off tonight at Xbox FanFest, where attendees will be the first to jump in and experience Firefight across latest maps and armed with plenty of weapons to help even the odds." It seems there's already a playable build of the mode, then.

It's worth noting that this is quite an odd news blast from Xbox, since the last official information we heard about the Halo brand was that the next major Halo game being developed by Activision, as Halo Studios all but closes as part of Microsoft's Xbox 'restructuring' that saw one key member behind Halo: Campaign Evolved promoted and laid off within the same week. As things stand, we don't know anything specific about the future of the series, but there are plenty of rumours that the next title will be a reboot developed by Call of Duty's Sledgehammer Games.

It's been fairly busy 24 hours for Xbox: as well as this Halo update, we've heard from Asha Sharma as she celebrated the 25th anniversary of Xbox by seemingly going all-in on Gen AI. Elsewhere, we got the announcement that Wolfenstein 3 is in development over at MachineGames, headed up by Hugo Martin.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
  • Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
  • A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A major research review led by Curtin University has found that people with type 2 diabetes face a significantly higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. The findings provide a clearer picture of the connection between diabetes and Alzheimer's, including how much the risk increases and how frequently new cases occur.

Researchers analyzed data from 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. They estimated that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes, approximately 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease over the course of one year.

A separate analysis found that people with type 2 diabetes had a 53 percent higher adjusted relative risk of developing Alzheimer's compared with those without the condition.

Understanding the Link Between Diabetes and Alzheimer's.

Study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an NHMRC Investigator Fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health, explained that the findings offer a more precise understanding of Alzheimer's risk among people with type 2 diabetes.

Unlike previous research reviews that often examined multiple forms of diabetes or dementia together, this analysis concentrated specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease. It also measured how frequently people with diabetes developed Alzheimer's, providing an additional perspective on the connection between the two conditions.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Dr. Adewuyi stated.

"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often upcoming cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes.".

The study, "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy.

10 Best N64 Racing Games That Still Hold Up Today

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that let's just get something out of the way quickly – you don't necessarily have to be great at a genre of games to enjoy playing them.
  • Recent findings suggest that most of the time I spent with racing games was on older consoles, most especially the Nintendo 64.
  • There's a lot of great games here, and so to avoid unnecessary bias, I've ranked them in large part based on their review score aggregates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that let's just get something out of the way quickly – you don't necessarily have to be great at a genre of games to enjoy playing them. I mean, sure, I'm quite good at platformers and deckbuilders, and play a ton of those. But if I just stuck with them, I'd get bored eventually. Which is why I enjoy genres I'm not particularly good at, like racing games.

Recent findings suggest that most of the time I spent with racing games was on older consoles, most especially the Nintendo 64. I clocked tons and tons of hours in many of them back then, and not just the most generic car racing games. I also played snowboarding games, water sports and even futuristic race car rallies. And honestly, every game on this N64 list still holds up today.

There's a lot of great games here, and so to avoid unnecessary bias, I've ranked them in large part based on their review score aggregates. Though in some cases, I did shuffle the order a bit when common sense called for it. So get ready, get set, and let's go through some epic N64 racing games!

Nintendo doesn't always have the most luck with launch titles, at least when they're not heavy hitters like Mario or Zelda. Which is why I was so delighted with Pilotwings 64 heralding the new console. It was very stylish, and built on the previous SNES adventure in great ways.

Industry observers note that your goal is to prove your stuff to earn a variety of pilot licenses in the game, and you'll have to accomplish some challenging feats. Those include autogyro, jet pack and hang gliding, even a human cannonball. Feats that aren't for the timid.

Even though the game is graphically less impressive today, the core gameplay still holds up, and offers a robust challenge and plenty of bonus activities for players. And thanks to the hard work Paradigm put in researching military vehicles and flight sims, Pilotwings 64 is just as relevant today as it was back then.

It highlights the breadth of the racing game library on the N64 when the first futuristic racer isn't F-Zero X, but instead is Extreme-G. Which isn't a dig, mind you, since both games offered a lot. But for this particular adventure, the highlights were some really epic weapons like homing missiles and laser mines, as well as really innovative, gravity defying courses.

The game also featured frenetic deathmatches, which made sense on paper, but in execution were a bit muddled. Sure, there's the likes of capture the flag, competitive racing and battle mode, but they were less fun than they were stress inducing.

It has been revealed that the biggest reason Extreme-G isn't ranked higher on this list is likely due to the graphics, which were fine but not overly impressive or creative. Still, if you had a need for speed and didn't mind using powerful weapons, this was a thrilling adventure.

While your mileage with arcade machines may vary, generally speaking they're massive, bold and visually impressive. And that goes double for racing games like San Francisco Rush 2049. Thankfully, they ported it to the N64, and brought high-octane energy to Nintendo's console.

Industry observers note that what was most impressive about this adventure on consoles is that you could extend wings from your vehicles and glide in mid-air. You'll mostly use that in the stunt mode to rack up crazy points as you do complex maneuvers.

According to recent reports, best of all, you had a lot to unlock in San Francisco Rush 2049, including new cars and tracks. Meaning that even now, this is a racing game you'll be spending a lot of time playing on the Nintendo 64 and even PC.

Since the developer of the Wipeout series was owned by Sony Computer Entertainment, it makes sense most of the games weren't on Nintendo consoles. The one exception was Wipeout 64. While perhaps not a true sequel to Wipeout 2097, this standalone Nintendo adventure offered a lot to enjoy.

Perhaps the most impressive way Wipeout 64 differentiated itself from the others in the series was a split screen allowing up to 4 players to play together. Even with that aside, the game offered robust anti-gravity racing and truly superior track design.

Industry observers note that if you enjoy racers with a variety of weapons, great tracks and a variety of gameplay modes, this N64 game had you covered. That said, perhaps the graphics were a step down from some of the other entries, but this was still a remarkably fun game.

Much as I love Nintendo, sometimes you have to wait a long while between sequels. Zelda fans know what I'm talking about, but even they didn't have to wait as long for a sequel as fans of the original Excitebike on the NES. 16 years later, it got its first sequel in Excitebike 64.

As you might expect, the jump from 2D to 3D was a substantial one, and you're capable of epic tricks in Excitebike 64. Brake, slide, turbo boost and even tilt the bike in midair, there's a lot of options. Better yet, the various playable athletes have distinct stats, allowing players to pick the one that works best with their style.

According to recent reports, my favorite aspect of the game is playing through the extensive season mode, unlocking new content along the way. But the one part of the game that really sets it apart is using the track editor to make your own insane obstacle courses.

Racing games on Nintendo consoles often lean into the fantastical, patterning themselves after the likes of Mario Kart. But one that really took a significant swing was Diddy Kong Racing. Not only did it feature different vehicles ranging from car to hovercraft to aeroplane, but there were also several different drivers and even a story involving the nefarious Wizpig.

Like any of the Donkey Kong games, there's a lot of unlockables here, including obtaining amulet pieces to battle the true final boss. And if that wasn't enough, you'll even deal with actual boss battles of sorts, and use balloons to gain a huge variety of powerups, ranging from missiles to speed boosts and shields.

Sources indicate that best of all, Diddy Kong Racing was quite pretty for the time, and the graphical style still looks great years later. Sure, it could get a bit repetitive, but this was still a really outstanding game you'd need to play on Nintendo 64.

Industry observers note that I mentioned earlier that I'm not the best at racing games, but I'm especially bad when they're on water. Which perhaps makes Wave Race 64 especially intimidating. That noted, if you put in enough practice time, even a rookie at the genre would find themselves loving this innovative and stunt-filled racing adventure.

Playing against the clock while trying to steer your way around buoys and avoid the hazing of your opponent could be really tough. If you're skilled, you'll power up and go even faster, but if you fail, you'll get way behind. Thankfully, though, this is a quite attractive N64 game which is even better when racing against a friend.

If you're more skilled at racing than me, you'll probably adore Wave Race 64. It's the sort of retro that still holds up today, and it offers a phenomenally fun time, assuming you can react swiftly to the choppy waters.

Even though I never played any skateboarding games, I really adored Snowboard Kids. I'm not sure what it was about this N64 adventure, but it hooked me hard. Maybe it was the cute, cartoony graphics, or the simple yet well balanced gameplay. But this was one of those games I found myself playing again and again.

Recent findings suggest that the simple hook of the game is doing tricks while airborne to get coins, and then using them to buy powerups on tracks. You can have active and support items, such as hurling rocks at your opponents or turning temporarily invisible.

Perhaps the most surprising aspect of Snowboard Kids was that it was published by Atlus, who are usually known for JRPGs. But this is just one of those games that is still a ton of fun today, which I can attest to having played it recently with my close friends on their N64.

Even though I'm not amazing at racing games, I spent many, many hours playing Mario Kart 64. I barely touched Super Mario Kart, didn't do much with the later entries, but that N64 game was one I kept returning to with friends.

There was just something about this game that made it one of the most iconic entries in the longrunning series. Maybe it was the quirky cast of Mario characters, maybe it was tracks like Rainbow Road. But this was a truly fun racing game that appealed to players of various abilities.

Industry observers note that mix in various engine classes, a wide class of racers and amazingly fun attack items, and you have a great game in Mario Kart 64. But if that wasn't enough, it also features some of the best courses in the series, complete with really catchy tunes.

If you have a need for speed, you need look no further than F-Zero X. This futuristic series featured some of the most blisteringly fast courses and crazy racers you'll see in any series. And honestly, F-Zero X is still probably one of the best racers ever. So even though it's shameful we haven't gotten a sequel, you might not need it either.

Recent findings suggest that death Race offered a truly unhinged way to play the game, and the randomness of X-Cup could keep you playing the game for a long time. So even though it's not the most graphically impressive game, the high framerate and fantasically weird drivers made this a worthy contender.

Industry observers note that plasma Powered hovercars turned made racing even more fun, and so long as you can keep up, you'll find one of the best racers ever in F-Zero X. Here's hoping it gets an even better followup on modern consoles one day.

  • Industry observers note that 'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since they released The Outer Worlds 2 around this time last year, the world has rather turned upside down for Obsidian. The studio lost a chunk of staff to Microsoft's mass layoffs and have pivoted to making a new Fallout game as a smaller group shoved underneath Bethesda in Xbox's corporate structure.

Recent findings suggest that given all that, The Outer Worlds 2's two-part story expansion is likely arriving in vastly different circumstances than those the studio might've imagined when they began sketching out DLC looks. Part one of the expansion, dubbed Side Effects Guaranteed, is set to release early next month.

Industry observers note that 'Oof, that looks a lot like it's been given what could turn out to be a death spot parked right in the aftermath of GTA 6's initial launch on consoles' is what I thought when I first saw that Side Effects Guaranteed's launch date is December 2nd. That stated, Obsidian have also made clear that a second DLC in the two-part narrative expansion to the sci-fi RPG is set to follow in spring 2027. So if this does turn out to be the end of the series, with a third Outer Worlds game currently looking very unlikely following the substantial upheaval I mentioned in the intro, at least it won't risk being totally obscured by a Rockstar crime game-shaped eclipse.

As for what this first dose of extra Outer Worlds 2 has in store for December, Obsidian summed it up as follows:.

Sources indicate that as you pursue the cure and set course for Elysium, an area home to former subjects of base game authoritarian collectivist faction the Protectorate, you'll be faced with the choice of whether to side with Gordon Hazen or Algernon Lankester. Both are agents of black market smuggling organisation Sub Rosa, with one sounding like the goody-two-shoes diplomatic type and the other wanting to "exploit the subjects for his own personal gain". Sounds more Saturday morning cartoon than serious RPG story with serious choices, but that's always tended to be how The Outer Worlds leans.

Recent findings suggest that rounding out the expansion are latest enemies, gear, flaws which give your character build a funky twist, and a bumping up of the level cap from from 30 to 36. Fittingly given I'm writing this on Skyrim's 15th birthday, one of the new flaws is named 'Must Have Been the Wind' after the meme of enemies in the likes of Bethesda and Obsidian's games returning to chill mode after being shot in the face with an arrow or facing some other obvious sign they're under attack. To encourage folks to dive back in, The Outer Worlds 2 is getting options to respec your character's skills and edit how many skill points are dished out per level up via an patch alongside Side Effects Guaranteed.

According to recent reports, as much as I'm resigned to the series' likely fate as Obsidian return to Fallout and won't pretend The Outer Worlds 2 was great rather than good, I'm still hopeful it can go out with a bang in these two expansions, if indeed this is the studio's last trip to space for the foreseeable future. It's worth noting that if you bought The Outer Worlds 2's premium edition, these expansions are included as part of it and so will come to you at no extra cost.
